title: Mini Ruler Included
html:
I started teaching about the same time the TI graphing calculator appeared on the market. Much like databases, I fell in love with it immediately, and saw how they could be used to help students in a math class. One could quickly see what changing one variable does to a graph. A wonderful visual aid. For example, say someone gives you this equation: y = ax^2 + bx + c and says they will leave it up to you to decide if the a is positive or negative.What does that mean?

When A is positive the parabola opens up.

When A is negative the parabola opens down.

Why I am showing you a TI graphing calculator instead of a Casio graphing calculator is because Texas Instruments made it very easy for a teacher to get a suitcase full of them (30 calculators) for a month at no charge and very little paperwork. I simply signed a piece of paper. After a month I wrote TI a letter asking them if I could keep them a little bit longer and they said no problem. They did not seem concerned but I was, what if I had to send them back next week. They had me. I no longer wanted them, I needed them. I had to have them. No matter the cost.There was money in the shoebox but too many eyes were watching it, that was not an option. The solution hit me while standing in the calculator aisle at a store. So many to choose from. All about the same price. What makes a customer pick one over the other? “Mini Ruler Included!” if they are basically the same and one has a ruler included, why not pick that one?

All I wanted in return for this multi-million dollar idea, was a suitcase full of TI-82s.

I sent the idea to TI.

Fair enough, we are talking about a whole suitcase of calculators here.

“Convert one edge of quick Reference Card into a mini-ruler. English system on one side and metric system on the other side.”

Hmm. maybe a picture or two would have helped. How could they not see the value?

In the end, to secure my calculator habit, we had a faculty car wash.

title: The Parabola Tracer
html:
I thought it would be groovy to have a physical model to demonstrate the properties of a parabola.

First proto-typeUsed in classroom (still used today at South High)

But wait! Order now and receive this TI-84 ParabolaTracer simulator program absolutely free!

Program written using TI-82.

My plan was to get them into every math department in the world. At one point i inquired about buying an ad in the Mathematics Teacher. I could not justify the cost of a quarter page ad. So instead I planned on getting a booth at math conferences. Math teachers would come by and roll the ball, use the laser, and then say they want one. By the time they ran the TI-82 Parabola program (lesson plan included), they would demand one.

It was a good plan and it still is a good plan. The problem is i have no inventory. I do not have the skills to make them or mass produce them. I did show it to one company and when they gave me an estimate of what just the mold would cost i got scared and evidentily have stayed in that state.

title: Fire-Ups
html:
In the 1990s it was common practice for cheerleaders at Fargo South High School to put “Fire-ups” on the lockers of students on a given team. For example, on a Friday in the Fall, all of the football players would have a fire-up on their locker for the game that night courtesy of the cheerleaders. I was using a database to maintain logistics for the Tri-College Math Contest. At some point it occurred to me I had enough info to mass produce individualized fire-ups with the locker number at the bottom - very helpful for distribution. Here was the final design

memory_1

I remember it was after school and I was in the process of printing the fire-ups. Diane Bierwagen was still in the office and asked me what I was doing. I told her I was going to put fire-ups on the lockers of students attending the Tri-College Math Contest the next day. She put her stuff down and asked if she could help put them up. I said it was okay I could do it but she pressed and ended up taking half of them. I was greatly relieved. I was not looking forward to hunting down the lockers for 60+ students. I did not feel it was right to ask my colleagues to help me with a self-inflicted project. Not sure why that memory stays with me. Maybe that small act of kindness has stayed with me because of what it represents. I received all of the credit. No one knows Diane helped.

memory_2

I remember a student coming into my classroom crying or on the verge of crying. In an emotional state. He wanted to thank me for the fire-up. He had never received one before and it meant a great deal to him. Pretty sure I know why I remember that one.

The Tri-College Math Contest

What it is: students from around the region gather at one of the colleges and take a math based test.

How it works: NDSU, Moorhead State, and Concordia are the participating colleges and use this rotation

  • One year host the event

  • One year write questions for the event

  • One year do nothing.

I believe this setup is one of the main reasons the contest has been sustainable. I used this model to promote MetroTechCamp.

College - game day

Me - practice for game day.

sidenote_1

Probably not going to use but spent time on it so not deleting it yet 🙂

While preparing for this book I was looking for an example of the fire-up. I spotted Kane Olson. Immediately makes me smile. In class I used to sing/say the phrase from the coconut song “you put the lime in the coconut…”. I remember Kane coming to class one day and presenting me with a CD with the coconut song on it. What a wonderful thing to do. So thoughtful and at such a young age.

title: The Pi Poster
html:
One year during the “Memorizing the Digits of Pi” contest (invented by the inventor of the durow dot), a student named Jake Enget memorized 1001 digits of pi. This feat made the AP news service, which led to the world knowing Fargo celebrates pi day. Exhibit A. A professor from somewhere in Oregon read the article in their local newspaper and contacted me. We started to converse. I shared my failed attempts at trying to print out thousands of digits of pi on one piece of paper. He exclaimed he had a poster with the first 100,000 digits of pi in which he gave his graduate students. He laced up his shoes and made the trek to Fargo to pass the scrolls to me. The tradition survived, nay, thrived. From that point on, the pi poster became the graduation gift I gave my students. For over a decade I was reassured by students these posters, posters secured by blood sweat and tears (much like the good job pencils), hung proudly on their wall. And yet, like you, I have no evidence of this.

When I left the classroom, I laced up my relatively new shoes, leaned across to the cubicle diagonal of mine, and passed the baton to Nancy. When Nancy retired in 02026 she could not afford shoes to lace, so simply leaned across to the cubicle diagonal of her, and passed the scrolls to Jessica. The low cost and grooviness will carry the tradition on for centuries to come. Much like the staff retirement frame.

title: Grading the Same Test
html:
As of 2026-07-21.

I do not think this vignette will make the blook. I do not like it anymore. I do like thought 1 though. I like my dans super valu reference.

Nexus

During the summer of some year, I was in Minot, North Dakota working on getting my masters in math teaching (salary scale was higher for those with a master degree). It was a good opportunity to do an experiment. I asked a fellow math teacher in Fargo who was teaching summer school to send me a copy of a student’s test (without name) so I could have my colleagues in Minot grade it separately. I wondered how close we would all be in scoring.

Memory 1

One teacher. I cannot remember who but I do know I really liked him. I found him very interesting. He literally graded the student’s test right in front of me. He marked them either right or wrong. No partial credit at all. None. It was not a multiple choice test. I wonder if he ever changed that practice. Seems so extreme to me. Some of those problems involved three or four steps. If a student showed all of their steps and for the last step had, say, 5 - 3 = 3 it was my practice to not take any points off. An astute reader will note I cowardly chose 5 - 3 = 3 instead of 3 - 5 = 2. I can explain my cowardliness but thy margin is too narrow to contain it.

Memory 2

I published my findings. And in that email, I put the city of the teacher and the grade they gave the test. I cannot remember the rules I used but I do recall them ranging from C to F. Now at this point our astute readers will have joined our hopeful readers and think this is the end of memory 2, since I just used the words remember and recall. It is not. Think of it as a memory within a memory (like that movie where they go into other people’s dream. I remember [oh my. A memory within a memory within a memory] at some point giving up trying to understand the movie and just sat back and hoped for the best). Anyway, the official memory 2 is sitting in a south high math department meeting and Milo Benson holding up my published work (he printed the email) and saying “it says here Fargo scored it a ? (cannot remember and not important). I don’t remember grading any test?” I had not given any thought to how it looked on paper without context. I screwed up. I was mortified. I took full responsibility but the damage was done. Failure can be brutal on the psyche.

Thought 1

I feel most of the educators I have met were involved in activities when they, themselves, were in high school. It was common to hear colleagues exchange their own high school experience/involvement in a given activity (sports,academics,arts…). I spent all my after school time and weekends at Dan's Super Valu. Where you’re always first.

title: The Pep Song
html:
I remember watching a soccer game late one night in my apartment on TV - a TV which at the time would take an entire wrestling team to move - and noticing basically the whole crowd singing the same song. I thought that was very groovy. So based on my 7th chair trombone experience, I wrote this pep song with the idea of the whole south high section singing in unison, or dare I dream, harmony.

The music in the video is a live take. The south high band is playing the music, the south high choir is singing, and I am “conducting”.

The animation was done by one of my students at the time. I have no idea how she did it. Keep in mind it was at a time when I had to wait until 10 pm (our tribal rule) to connect to the internet with my 56k modem.

Play pep song (nothing happens until second 19 or 20 and then repeats a couple of times so not very long. You can do it. It is less than a minute. You take out the first 20 seconds and the last say,15 seconds (it repeats) and you are down to about 21 seconds [seinfeld reference?]. Well worth the time investment. I will await your return.)

See, now that wasn’t all that bad. It gets a lot worse.

Anyway, with demo tape in hand I made a pitch to school administration to perform the pep song at a pep assembly. Permission was granted and cheerleaders began making posters. As I recall, we had some of the band members there to play, I had the microphone and led the singing, and cheerleaders held up posters with the words on them. The fewer people still alive, the better that performance gets.

Actually it really did go well at the pep assembly but it failed to catch on. Why did it not catch on? I am glad you asked. We know the lyrics and music are brilliant so why did it not prevail? I have ideas but in the end, we will never know what the students did wrong. Go Bruins!

title: The Tri-College Math Contest
html:
The Tri-College Math Contest is still in existence as of this writing (02026).

What it is: students from around the region gather at one of the colleges and take a math based test.

How it works: NDSU, Moorhead State, and Concordia are the participating colleges and use this rotation

  • One year host the event

  • One year write questions for the event

  • One year do nothing

I believe this setup is one of the main reasons the contest has been sustainable. I used this model to promote MetroTechCamp.

When I first got involved with taking students to the Tri-College Math contest, it seemed every year WaterView School District was towards the top of the leaderboard. I decided to use them as a motivator for my students. Beat WaterView.

The first year we trained for the Tri-College Math contest, South swept. Something like 6 out of top 10 were South High students. Unheard of. And probably still very rare if at all.

It was magical. I still have a snapshot in my head of being in the Concordia auditorium and hearing south high again and again.

-not a proud moment with me and the media. I was very demanding they print the results (like they did the year before when it was not South High). My heart was in the right place, I was thinking about my students, just a terrible delivery system.

Math group had paid off!

I.e. I am amazing!!

Then I overheard a conversation in the main office. “This year’s class is academically exceptional…” something like that. I remember thinking. Wait. so you are not giving me any credit. Nice. That statement turned out to be completely true. I had nothing to do with it. However, I did have something to do with putting fire-ups on lockers.

–so I do not forget. I grew up with the 9th grade class. I went to discovery the first year it opened. The math department chair, for whatever reason, put most of the really “high flyers” in my class. I did not know that.

title: The Pi Cake
html:
After the maiden voyage of pi day, we set our sights on the Guinness Book of Records category for longest digits of pi on a cake. I was feeling pretty good about beating the old record because it did not exist since I just made up the category.

Preliminary feedback from the Guinness Book of Records made us very confident. It sounded like the novelty of what we were trying to do might make the book. Keep in mind, the book was a big deal at the time. If you asked one for the world record of paperclips linked together, they would need to refer to a physical book to find the answer. No internets yet. At this point we were pumped. We began to prepare the piCake. The representative would visually inspect the digits to make sure they were correct so we needed to be accurate/organized. There were many rules to explain to the Guinness person about their new category. It would be crushing to get this far only to be rejected because we had two digits in the wrong order.

Pi cake recipe (one segment)

Ingredients:

  • 1 12x8 cake pan.

  • Stuff for white cake

  • One segment worth of white frosting

Steps:

  1. Make cake, bake cake until done, frost cake

  2. Cover cardboard provided with tinfoil

  3. Cut cake into three equal rows, lay end to end on the cardboard, ice cake with the digits of pi provided.

  4. Don’t screw up the order of the digits. We are going for a record here.

Visual aids:

We planned for The Guinness Book of Records representative to arrive at 3:14 pm and announce our entry into the Guiness Book of Records.

I am thinking now would be a good time to point out I have been playing fast and loose with the facts. Need more here.

title: Good Job Pencils
html:
I thought it would be groovy if every student at some point in the year received a personalized pencil for doing well (for them) on a test. I did not know how to do it so I asked my students. Dear reader. If in your head right now you are thinking of 3d printing. dude/dudette this was back when calculator watches ruled the world. After a couple of brainstorming sessions with my classes it was decided I would try to burn the letters into the wood pencil. We were not quite sure how we were going to do it but we had a plan. I went to a thrift store in search of a typewriter I could dismantle. Such a simple sentence. No thought of what anguish it would cause. I went into that thrift store blissfully. I left that thrift store with a typewriter, a toolbelt, a pair of shoes which looked relatively new, and a toaster addiction that would last years and end tragically. Once home, I garnished my toolbelt and dismantled the typewriter. I then held the letter G against the stove burner with a pair of pliers. After about 10 seconds I looked to my left and saw no one, then looked to my right and saw no one, then turned on the stove. It did not matter. Not even in the ballpark. Even if it would have burned into the wood pencil, it was not sustainable or scalable. I shared the failure with my students and then sometimes, prior to deriving the quadratic formula, we would do more brainstorming. After a couple more failed attempts we found a solution by cutting a slot in the rubber the shape of a wooden pencil. I would put the pencil in the slot and then just pound the heck out of the letter “G” and then forward a space and pound the heck out of the letter “o” going forward a space etc. I tested a variety of pencil brands and finally bought in bulk the type which displayed the letters the best.

Once the pencils were in production we needed rules on how one might obtain a pencil and what is written upon said pencil. For example, a student who did really well compared to their other tests then they would get a “Good job name here” pencil. If a student scored 100% then they automatically received a “Super job name here pencil”. The students loved it. They started pumping themselves up to do the practice so they could get a personal best on the next test to get a pencil. It also helped the culture of our classroom.

One rule I had that I did not share with my students was every student must get at least one pencil during the course. I did not like the idea of someone trying all term and not getting some kind of positive reinforcement. The hard part was knowing when to give the pencil. Do I give them a pencil for the 68% on this test or see if the next test, the last test, they get, say a 70%? It was a little stressful and making pencils ate up most of my Sunday but it was reaping benefits in my classroom and therefore worth the time and effort.

The next year I shared the rules with my new students and started distributing pencils, just like last year. At first they were receptive to it. They liked getting the pencil. And then I noticed they started to complain about the pencil. “I can barely see the letters”, “Why is my name slanted?”, “You should color these letters. I can barely see them”. Etc. Shortly after that, I stopped making them. I was not mad at all. It was not the pencil, it was being part of it. Those names were just as faint and slanted last year.

title: Fermat’s Last Theorem
html:
It was Thursday 1996. It was an important day. We would tackle the crucial life skill of deriving the quadratic formula.

I was just starting class: “Hello everyone! At this time I would like to announce my retirement, but I cannot, so open your books to page” — I would never get the page number out. I was interrupted by a breaking story.

How could this day get any bigger?

And then we heard the news. Andrew Wiles had proven Fermat’s Last Theorem!

And there was great rejoicing.

Students started asking questions. Who is Andrew Wiles? What did he do? How did he do it? Will it be on the test? Are we having corndogs for lunch today? Can we leave for lunch early today since it is corndog Thursday? It is looking bad out there. Do you think we will get out early today? Yeah Durow, are you parting your hair differently today?

The questions just poured out.

I was not sure I was stable enough to teach, so I covered it by suggesting we watch TV. Maybe Prairie Public might have the inside scoop.

The reaction from my students made the shape of a quadratic—how apropos—with x-intercepts at “deriving the quadratic formula” and “Prairie Public” and the vertex at “watch TV.” I will leave it to the reader to decide if a is positive or negative.

y = ax2 + bx + c

I was looking for the TV remote when one student voiced opposition. He wanted to know why we had to watch this Wiles guy on TV when we did not get to watch TV when the planes crashed into the Twin Towers.

Now the astute reader might have picked up on the fact that 9/11 happened in 2001 and our story is from 1996.

Well done! You have caught me in a web of lies.

But since we are here...

I was teaching at the board when 9/11 happened. I turned on the TV and we watched for a couple of minutes. I did not know what to do. No clue.

Maybe there is something in our teacher manual. Where is my teacher manual? Okay, think. I could ask Nancy. I know she is probably reading hers right now. I could, but that would lead to a ten-minute dissertation on the importance of being organized. I have attended that seminar multiple times. Let’s make that Plan F.

Oh, I know where it is!

Okay kids, be careful. This table is going to be wobbly for a while.

So what do I look for? See, this is why we need to make these documents electronic.

In the end, I figured they would be playing the video clips on repeat, so I turned off the TV and continued with deriving the quadratic formula.

I realize I am making light of an extremely sad day and a very scary time in our country. I was there as well, and like everyone else, I was trying to figure out what to do.

I still think about that decision. I am not concerned whether it was right or wrong—pretty sure there was no definitive right or wrong thing to do—just the strangeness of the situation.

Oh my. I just realized I have not gotten to the story part yet. Think Teddy.

When the mood hit, prior to starting the lesson for the day, I would point to the famous mathematicians I had so painstakingly taped to the wall and would decree:

“Andrew Wiles’s picture will now be taped next to the other people on this wall. Some of these people are over 2,000 years old. Andrew Wiles is ten years older than me. How groovy is that!”

I would then share snippets of The Proof from the 1997 episode of Nova with the class.

At one point, Mr. Wiles becomes emotional and begins to cry. On cue, there would be a multitude of giggles, snickers, and such.

I would then rewind the tape, turn on the lights, and continue deriving the quadratic formula.

Several days would pass. Then, prior to starting the lesson for the day, I would pop in a video showing Michael Jordan’s reaction right after winning the championship. He hugs the trophy, kisses it, and cries.

No giggles. No mocking. Just a bunch of heads bobbing and reminiscing.

I remind them of their reaction when Andrew Wiles cried and then continue deriving the quadratic formula.

title: The Postcard
html:
I was involved with TechCamp for over 20 years. For the last nine years we called it MetroTechCamp because West Fargo, Moorhead, and DGF joined us. I was a strong advocate of making it happen. I thought there were multiple reasons why we should try to expand TechCamp to the metro area. Just one example before we begin our story. It takes several departments within each District to hold an event like MetoTechCamp. Which means staff members from each district end up meeting their counterparts in other districts. So when in six months, there is a state issue, our staff members might have someone they can call to compare notes. Anyway, that has nothing to do with the story nor does it give you any idea what MetroTechCamp is.Hmm. Tired of writing. So with the end of the beginning credits in Monty Python and the Search for the Holy Grail in mind: MetroTechCamp is a 2-3 day conference for K-12 Teachers.

I thought it would be groovy to find clever ways to help promote teachers coming back to MetroTechCamp in subsequent years - repeat business. Districts used PD budgets so metro teachers could attend MetroTechCamp free of charge. For those interested, we did offer continuing ed credits via NDSU - who did a wonderful job of keeping the cost of credits down for teachers to pay. Nancy and I both took advantage of the inexpensive credit over the years.

This postcard triggered an idea. We could send a postcard to those who had attended MetroTechCamp.

A lot of work was done. Think of your favorite montage with the music ending here:

.

Emily worked with the Davies something group. She gave each of them a stack of postcards and a couple of prompts of what to write.

Once postcards had been signed, we needed to deliver them. We could have interschool mailed them but Emily and I decided we would put them in the teacher mailboxes ourselves. We started at 8:00 am and did not finish until 4:30 pm. Long day but Emily made it an absolutely wonderful day.

–

The next year whenever I was in a school for a meeting, I kept an eye open for any evidence of the postcards. It was fun to find them. I am calling it a win. Having said that, we never did it again. And if we did, Emily and I both agreed, interschool mail sounded like a great idea.

title: The Pi Song
html:
Both Nancy and I are from Bismarck, North Dakota. We have two children, which translates to many trips to Bismarck to see grandmas and grandpas.

The radio had not been invented yet, so sometimes I would explain to the kids how to derive the quadratic formula, while other times Nancy would give a dissertation to all of us on the importance of organizing your materials.

We were in the van on the interstate heading to Bismarck because my mom's neighbor's niece was there, and my mom thought we might want to meet her.

Steven: Thank you, Nancy! I had not thought about organizing toys by width. Interesting.

Emily: I organize my toys by height!

Steven: Well, Mom thinks you're stupid.

Alex, to himself: No, no, no. I see where this is going. Mom is going to talk about how toys can also be organized by weight, which will trigger something in Dad. He will start talking about how all these different ways of organizing one's toys remind him of the multitude of ways the quadratic formula can be derived. Then the lecture/torture begins. I can't do it. Wait, I have an idea!

Alex: Yeah, look! Mile marker 314! You know, Mom and Dad, you two should write a song about pi while we drive to Bismarck.

Emily, to herself: Brilliant! Bless you, brother! This will keep those two quiet for most of the trip. I could sense trouble when Mom started talking about toy weight. I knew Dad would figure out a way to start talking about the quadratic formula. He's an idiot.

Camera work was done by Kathy Fisher. Nancy displayed the words while I sang and played the guitar.

On Pi Day, I would bring a TV/VCR combination unit to the commons and play the Pi Song on repeat. Student pleas to turn it off for a while went unheard.

excerpt: A family road trip to Bismarck takes an unexpected turn when Alex devises a brilliant plan to keep Mom from talking about organization and Dad from launching into yet another explanation of the quadratic formula: convince them to write a song about pi. title: Papergate
html:
Like most teachers, I was not a big fan of correcting practice (homework).

My policy was simple. If you handed in your practice and spelled your name correctly, you got the points.

The practice problems looked like the quiz problems, which looked like the test problems. I stayed away from trick questions. No surprises. If you understood the practice, you would understand the quiz. If you understood the quiz, you would understand the test.

The practice was for the students, not for me.

A couple of times I tried eliminating the practice grade altogether.

It failed.

Students actually asked me to start collecting it again because, without the points, many of them simply stopped doing the practice.

So we needed Plan B.

I decided the process itself needed to be better.

Students were only allowed to work one problem per box. Every sheet included a graphing grid. The paper was three-hole punched so it would fit neatly into binders and eliminate those ragged notebook edges that seemed to multiply overnight.

I searched for paper like that.

It did not exist.

So I made my own.

Students could immediately tell if they had skipped a step because every problem occupied its own space. It kept their work organized, made graphing convenient, and made it much easier for me to glance through a page and spot where someone was struggling.

Since I had custom math paper printed, I charged one dollar for a pack of 100 sheets.

Me, during a future job interview:

"...anyway, since I had math paper custom made, I charged a dollar per pack."

Smeds: "I don't believe Durow. It's a scam. He's charging those kids and pocketing the money."

(turns to Jessica)

"Remember that Tuesday he was wearing new socks? And...and...his shoes. They looked relatively new. Remember?"

Jessica: "Hmm... His shoes did look relatively new."

Back to the interview.

"To be honest, if students didn't have a dollar, I usually told them to pay me later."

I did not keep very good records.

In fact, I probably paid for most of the paper myself.

Or, more accurately, I will pay for most of the paper myself.

I still have not received the bill.

Fortunately, I still have a shoebox full of money ready and waiting.
